Washington Liquor Licenses and LCB Compliance: The Rules That Catch Owners Off Guard

8 min read·Justin D. Leigh, Attorney-at-Law

You have a purchase and sale agreement for a neighborhood bar, a closing date, and a price allocation with a line item for the liquor license. Or you run a brewery, and a restaurant has offered to build a dedicated tap wall if you help pay for the sign. Both are ordinary commercial instincts, and both run into the regulatory architecture around alcohol here. A Washington liquor license is not an asset that travels with a business, and the rules about who may give what to whom reach conduct that looks like nothing more than marketing.

Who regulates alcohol in Washington, and under what law

Title 66 RCW is the state's alcohol statute, built on the 1933 act that may be cited as the Washington State Liquor Act. RCW 66.98.010. It is administered by a three-member board known as the Washington state liquor and cannabis board, with broad rulemaking authority. RCW 66.08.012; RCW 66.08.030. The Board's rules are Title 314 WAC, and they hold most of the operational detail, so an owner who reads only the statute misses half the regime.

License categories turn on what a business does with alcohol rather than what it calls itself. On-premises retail includes the spirits, beer, and wine restaurant license and the beer and wine restaurant license, while off-premises retail includes the grocery store license and the beer and wine specialty shop license. RCW 66.24.400; RCW 66.24.320; RCW 66.24.360; RCW 66.24.371. Producers have their own tiers, with separate licenses for microbreweries, domestic wineries, distilleries, and craft distilleries, each carrying tasting-room conditions written into the statute. RCW 66.24.244; RCW 66.24.170; RCW 66.24.140; RCW 66.24.145. A business has the privileges its license grants and nothing broader, so a taproom that begins hosting ticketed dinners may have outrun its license.

The three-tier system is more subtle than people expect

Most people understand the three-tier system as a flat prohibition, with producers, distributors, and retailers kept separate and nobody owning across the lines. In Washington that is no longer accurate. The Legislature found that the historical total prohibition on holding an interest in one tier while holding an interest in another "is unduly restrictive." RCW 66.28.280.

What replaced it is a standard rather than a bar. It is lawful for an industry member to hold a direct or indirect financial interest in a retailer, and for a retailer to hold an interest in an industry member, unless the interest has resulted or is more likely than not to result in undue influence or in an adverse impact on public health and safety. RCW 66.28.290(1), (2). That is better news for business planning and worse news for certainty, because the test is qualitative and somebody else applies it.

Two rules keep the standard from collapsing. First, except for promotional items specifically allowed by RCW 66.28.310, no industry member may advance and no retailer may receive money or money's worth "under an agreement written or unwritten or by means of any other business practice or arrangement." RCW 66.28.305. That language reaches informal arrangements, and it is what turns a brewery paying for a bar's sign into a problem. Second, the Board decides, because any person may request a Board determination on a financial interest, and if the Board finds undue influence it may issue an administrative violation notice or a notice of intent to deny a license, and where the transaction has already closed it may require that the transaction be rescinded or otherwise undone. RCW 66.28.300.

The advertising rules work the same way, barring a retail licensee's name from a manufacturer's, importer's, or distributor's advertising and permitting a brand name in a retailer's own advertising only where nothing of value was exchanged for the mention. WAC 314-52-090.

Applying: the local authority notice and the objection window

Every license issues in the name of the applicant, and the holder may not allow anyone else to use it. RCW 66.24.010(1). The Board may inspect the premises, inquire into all matters connected with its construction and operation, and consider prior criminal conduct and violation history. RCW 66.24.010(2). A sole proprietor applicant must have lived in Washington at least a month, and a corporation or LLC must be formed here or hold a certificate of authority. RCW 66.24.010(1)(a), (d). No applicant may exercise any privilege until the Board approves the application. WAC 314-07-015(3).

Applicants underestimate the objection track. The city or town, or the county legislative authority, may file written objections with the Board against the applicant or the premises within twenty days after the notice of application is transmitted. RCW 66.24.010(8)(c). The Board must also notify churches, schools, and designated public institutions within five hundred feet, and it may not license previously unlicensed premises within five hundred feet of a tax-supported public elementary or secondary school, measured between entrances, if the school objects in writing within twenty days. RCW 66.24.010(9)(a). A lease signed before anyone measured that distance is a lease on space that may not be licensable.

The licensed premises is a boundary, not an address

The Board's rules define licensed premises as all areas under the licensee's legal control that are available to or used by customers or employees in the conduct of business operations, and they add that specific alcohol consumption areas must be approved by the Board, which makes the approved floor plan part of the license. WAC 314-01-005(1).

Changes to that footprint require approval from the licensing division. Any alteration affecting the size of the customer service area requires approval, the licensee submits two sets of floor plans, and service in the altered area may begin only after the local liquor enforcement officer inspects it. WAC 314-03-300(1). Excluding patrons under twenty-one, reclassifying a lounge for an event, extending service outdoors, and sharing a service area with a non-licensee each have their own rule. WAC 314-03-300(2) through (4); WAC 314-03-200; WAC 314-03-215. Licensed premises are also open to inspection, and refusing to allow it is itself a violation. RCW 66.28.090.

A license does not come with the business

This is the most expensive misunderstanding in the field. Because a Washington liquor license issues in the name of the applicant, it does not convey by a bill of sale, and prior Board approval is required before an ownership change. WAC 314-07-080(1). A change in the qualifying persons of a sole proprietorship or a partnership requires a new application at the annual fee, while a change in a corporation's officers or stockholders, or in an LLC's members or managers, requires the corresponding application. WAC 314-07-080(1). Stock and unit transfers are tracked cumulatively against a ten percent threshold, so a series of small transfers can trigger an obligation no single transfer would, and who counts as an owner is governed by the true party of interest rules. WAC 314-07-080(3); WAC 314-07-035.

Temporary retail licenses exist, and they are what buyers reach for when they assume a license can be handed over at closing, but a temporary license is a discretionary Board action with its own grounds for denial and revocation. WAC 314-07-055; WAC 314-07-060. The closing date and the licensing timeline are two different schedules, and an agreement that treats them as one has allocated a risk nobody priced.

When an administrative violation notice arrives

Enforcement runs on a short clock. After the Board notifies a licensee of an alleged violation, the licensee has twenty days from receipt to do one of three things on the agency's form: accept the recommended penalty, request a settlement conference in writing, or request an administrative hearing in writing. WAC 314-29-005; WAC 314-29-010(1). Doing nothing is itself a choice with a consequence, because absent a response within twenty days the recommended suspension takes effect. WAC 314-29-010(2)(a).

A settlement conference is a real process. The licensee and a hearing examiner or enforcement captain discuss the circumstances, the recommended penalty, and any aggravating or mitigating factors, and a compromise the Board approves becomes part of the licensing history. WAC 314-29-010(3). That matters more than it looks, because penalties escalate with violation history. WAC 314-29-015. Formal action is an adjudicative proceeding under chapter 34.05 RCW, with one exception to a prior hearing: the Board may summarily suspend a license for up to one hundred eighty days on a finding that public health, safety, or welfare imperatively require emergency action. RCW 66.08.150(4).

Where this goes wrong

Buying a bar and assuming the license comes with it. Prior Board approval of the ownership change is required, and the new owner may not exercise any privilege until approval issues. WAC 314-07-080; WAC 314-07-015(3).

A tasting-room or event arrangement that crosses a tier. The money's worth prohibition and the advertising rules both reach the co-branded release party, the subsidized sign, and the offer to help with tap handles, and the Board can require a closed transaction to be undone. RCW 66.28.305; WAC 314-52-090; RCW 66.28.300.

Altering the premises first and asking later. Expanding a patio or adding a service bar changes the customer service area and requires approval, plans, and inspection before service begins. WAC 314-03-300(1).

Treating a violation notice as a parking ticket. The twenty-day window closes, the suspension attaches, and the history follows the license into the next matter.

Why this is lawyer work

The hard part is not reading any single rule. It is that the answer to a business question usually lives in three places at once, with a prohibition stated in Title 66 RCW, an exception defined in Title 314 WAC, and an agency practice about structure that neither document describes. Deal timing is the other recurring problem, because purchase agreements and financing commitments get signed on commercial schedules while licensing runs on its own.

About my practice
